prompt: What does `pip install --require-hashes -r requirements.txt` protect against?

options.text: Every listed package being free of known vulnerabilities
options.explanation: Hashes say nothing about vulnerabilities. A pinned, hash-matched package can still have a CVE; that is SCA's job.

options.text: Rejecting downloaded distributions that do not match an approved digest, such as an unexpected replacement file
options.explanation: Correct. pip compares each downloaded distribution with the allowed hashes for that requirement. Several hashes can approve platform variants; a matching finite digest is strong evidence rather than a proof of byte equality or content safety. Source-build dependencies need separate controls.

options.text: A malicious maintainer publishing a backdoor in the exact version you pinned
options.explanation: If the backdoored file was the one you hashed (as with xz 5.6.1 for anyone who pinned it), the hash matches. Hashes freeze content; they don't judge it.

options.text: Typosquatting, by checking that package names are spelled correctly
options.explanation: If you typed the typosquatted name into the file and hashed its file, pip would happily install it. Hashes don't check spelling.

workedExample: Hash-checking mode requires explicitly covered dependencies and accepted artifact hashes. Unexpected downloaded content is rejected, while a malicious artifact whose hash was approved still passes. Source-build dependencies and build execution require their own controls; prefer reviewed wheels or separately controlled builds when relevant.

link.title: pip: secure installs and hash-checking mode
